blogs.title: Writing Software Like Prose
blogs.subtitle: On why readability, naming conventions, and deliberate architecture matter more than clever one-liners in long-lived production systems.
blogs.coverCaption: Fig. 1 — Architectural harmony between domain layers.
blogs.excerpt: Most code is read far more often than it is written. Treating your codebase with the editorial discipline of an essay produces software that stands the test of time.

intro: Every software engineer eventually discovers that code is primarily a medium of human communication. Compilers are indifferent to indentation, elegance, or empathy. They translate byte for byte without opinion.
The real audience for any non-trivial codebase is the tired engineer opening your file six months from now — who is very likely to be yourself.

sections.heading: 1. The Grammar of Good Architecture
paragraphs: In literature, a well-structured essay unfolds logically: each paragraph presents a premise, develops it, and leads naturally to the next. High-performing software architectures mimic this exact rhythm.
When service layers speak clearly to data repositories, and domain models represent business realities without unnecessary translation indirection, cognitive friction dissolves.
sections.quote: Clear code is not the byproduct of brilliant brevity; it is the deliberate elimination of cognitive burden.

sections.heading: 2. Naming as Semantic Contract
paragraphs: Consider variable names. An abbreviation saves keystrokes today, but costs minutes of deciphering on every subsequent read.
A function name should read like an active sentence with clear intent and zero hidden side effects.

code.caption: Predictable naming vs. mysterious shorthand

content.conclusion: Building software like prose isn't about writing essays inside source files. It is about respecting the cognitive load of everyone who will touch your work tomorrow. When you prioritize clarity, empathy, and deliberate architecture, the software inevitably stands the test of time.
